title: Pasi Rautio appointed as a new Professor and the Director of the Arctic Centre
content:
26.10.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Interim Director | Arctic Centre

    Doctor of Philosophy and Adjunct Professor Pasi Rautio has been appointed for the position of Professor in Arctic Resilience and Adaption at the Arctic Centre of University of Lapland. The Professorship also includes the tasks of the Director of the Arctic Centre for the term lasting until the end of 2029.

    Rautio will begin in his position on 11.1.2027. Currently he works as a Research Professor of Silviculture in the Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) in Rovaniemi. The new professorship is part of the University of Lapland’s strategic choice of Global Arctic responsibility.

    Rautio earned his Doctor of Philosophy in Plant ecology at the University of Oulu, where he also holds a docentship of Plant and Environmental Ecology. For a long time, Rautio has worked in research assignments at the Natural Resources Institute Finland and at its predecessor Finnish Forest Research Institute (METLA). In addition, he has worked at the European Commission in Brussels and been involved in numerous international research projects and international networks within his field.

title: Nonfiction writers’ award for Markku Heikkilä
content:
26.10.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Head of Science Communications | Arctic Centre

    Head of science communications at the Arctic Centre, University of Lapland Markku Heikkilä is one of the recipients of Nonfiction writers’ award 2026.

    The annual Nonfiction writers’ awards were presented by The Association of Finnish Nonfiction Writers awards at the Helsinki Book Fair October 24, 2026. The award recipients were Kai Ekholm, Markku Heikkilä, Jenni Räinä, Ilkka Taipale ja Vappu Taipale. The awards were presented for the 26th time.

    The amount of the awards are 8,000 euros and are awarded in recognition of extensive and distinguished work in the field of non-fiction writing.

    Markku Heikkilä has worked as a head of science communications at the Arctic Centre since 2010. Before that he made a career as journalist in newspaper Kaleva in various positions between 1986–2010 where he also followed northern affairs closely.

title: Call for Session Proposals for the Rovaniemi Arctic Spirit Conference 2027 is now open
content:
28.10.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • We welcome proposals for sessions to be held during the Rovaniemi Arctic Spirit Conference which takes place in Rovaniemi, Finland on 24 – 26 May 2027.

    The conference is organized by the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland and the City of Rovaniemi with several partners.  This year the conference is organized with a main theme “Our Arctic Home and Its Sustainable Future”.

    The Arctic region is home to humans but also many other species — both now and for generations to come. The conference will highlight different perspectives on how to ensure that the Arctic region remains a good place for everyone to live and call ‘home’.

    The first conference day is a policy day with keynotes and panels. The scientific and thematic sessions will be organized on the second day. We welcome proposals for sessions that can be comprised of oral presentations or panel/round table discussions.  

    The length of the sessions will most likely be 90 minutes, including sufficient time for Q&A or other forms of audience involvement. 

    Sessions should cover some elements of the sustainable future of the Arctic and follow for example one of these themes:

title: Leena Leppänen has been awarded the title of Docent at the Arctic Centre
content:
15.10.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Visiting Researcher | Arctic Centre, University of Lapland

    Leena Leppänen, Doctor of Philosophy, has been awarded the title of Docent at the Arctic Centre of the University of Lapland starting November 1, 2026. The title of Docent is given in the field of Snow Physics.

    Leppänen’s research focuses on snow physics, snow microstructure, and snow measurements. She possesses extensive, over a decade long professional experience in snow research. She has done snow measurements in Lapland, Switzerland, Iceland, Svalbard, and Antarctica. Leppänen’s current research concerns the effects of water falling onto a snow surface, such as the changes in the snow microstructure.

    Leppänen received her doctorate in geophysics from the University of Helsinki in 2020. Her doctoral thesis investigated the measurement and modeling of seasonal snowpack properties using passive microwave observations.

title: H.M. King of Spain and the President of the Republic of Finland with their spouses visited the University of Lapland and Arktikum
content:
08.10.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Their Majesties King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain and the President of the Republic of Finland Alexander Stubb and his spouse Suzanne Innes-Stubb visited the University of Lapland on the 7th of October 2026.

    As part of the visit at the University of Lapland, a panel discussion was held, and His Majesty and the President of the Republic delivered their speeches on European security, global engagement and cooperation. Before the public event program included a visit to the Science Centre and Museum Arktikum.

    The high-level visit filled the Fellman Hall at the university’s main campus to capacity with students and staff members from the University of Lapland and the Lapland University of Applied Sciences as well as other invited guests. The event was opened with a panel discussion titled Bridging Europe’s Frontiers: Security and Cooperation from the Arctic to the Mediterranean and the Construction of European International Actorness.

title: A new publication examines the cumulative impacts of the green transition on traditional Sámi livelihoods
content:
30.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Researcher | Arctic Centre, the University of Lapland

    In Nordic cooperation made report “Towards understanding and managing cumulative impacts in Sápmi: approaches & collaboration – Workshop Report with focus on spatial data, reindeer and reindeer herding” explores the use of spatial data and methods in assessing cumulative impacts on traditional Sámi livelihoods.

    The impacts of the green transition on Sápmi and reindeer herding areas have been increasing due to factors such as forestry, rare-earth mineral mining, and the production of hydroelectric and wind power. The planning processes for these past, ongoing, and future projects are highly fragmented; consequently, the cumulative impacts of the projects and the perspectives of local people have not been adequately considered during the planning stages. Assessing the impacts of both historical and new activities in Sápmi requires concepts, frameworks, and tools capable of addressing cumulative impacts across space, time, sectors, and borders, as well as a stronger knowledge base to support just decision-making.

title: A new project focuses on the viability of volunteer work in northern regions
content:
21.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Project manager, PREPAREd | Arctic Centre, University of Lapland

    Senior Specialist, PREPAREd | Arctic Centre, University of Lapland

    The importance of volunteer action for societal preparedness and resilience is growing amid global polycrisis. Current global challenges are deeply interconnected and amplify one another, requiring new ways to approach crises and devise future pathways.

    A new international project, PREPAREd, led by the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland, examines how volunteering contributes to resilient societies and what support is needed to maintain viable volunteer organisations in a rapidly changing operating environment.

    Volunteers and civil society organisations form a vital, but often less visible, part of society’s capacity to function. Their work can be seen, for example, in preparedness, search-and-rescue activities, environmental protection, and support for local communities on an everyday basis, as well as during times of disruption and crisis. Volunteering is also a central aspect of an inclusive society, offering individuals a sense of belonging and opportunities for agency and lifelong learning.

title: EU leaders visited Arktikum as a part of the European Arctic Summit held in Rovaniemi
content:
17.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • The European Arctic Summit was held in Rovaniemi 13-14 September 2026, where EU leaders gathered to address issues related to the Arctic region.

    The geopolitical significance of the Arctic continues to grow rapidly, and the aim of the European Arctic Summit held in Rovaniemi was to strengthen the EU’s common strategic approach to the region. Arktikum served as a meeting venue for the summit, where the EU leaders also got to visit the Arctic Opposites science exhibition by the Arctic Centre with the executive producer Nicolas Gunslay.

    In addition, EU politicians discussed with local representatives about current Arctic questions such as the impacts of climate change and the perspectives of the Sámi People’s, the EU’s only Indigenous People, to the changing state of the region. The Rector of the University of Lapland Antti Syväjärvi and the President of the Sámi Parliament of Finland Pirita Näkkäläjärvi took part in these discussions held in Arktikum. The President Näkkälärvi emphasized to European heads of state that sustainable Arctic security can’t be achieved without the people of the Arctic and vibrant Indigenous peoples.

title: Collaboration to find solutions for waste management in Arctic municipalities
content:
16.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Postdoctoral Researcher | Arctic Centre

  • STRAWCO Project

    • Nadezhda Filimonova’s desire to use her research to bring tangible benefits to the residents of the Arctic led her to explore the challenges and solutions related to circular waste management.

    Nadezhda Filimonova’s path to a career as an Arctic researcher began to take shape early on. According to her own words, even before she was born.

    “My father worked as a polar researcher for over 40 years. Already in my early childhood, I heard fascinating stories about those distant places. The seed of my enthusiasm was probably planted back then.”

    During the early stages of her university studies in Sweden and Russia, Filimonova was more interested in the national level of Arctic politics, especially the geopolitical aspects. When attending a doctoral program in the United States, she ended up examining the Arctic region at city and regional levels.

title: New EU-funded project Beyond Arctic PASSION officially launched on 1st September, runs for four years
content:
10.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Beyond Arctic PASSION works to build a more coordinated Arctic Observing System of Systems to address the challenges in the Arctic region.

    For decades, scientists, Indigenous Peoples, local communities and governments have worked to build a more coordinated Arctic Observing System that connects people, knowledge and technology. Yet, the Arctic continues to change faster than our ability to observe it. Observations remain fragmented across nations, observing infrastructures, data systems and knowledge systems, limiting our ability to address the complex environmental and societal challenges facing the region.
